title: India's textile workers: a fabric of two million stories
author: Editorial Desk
summary: A look at the sector that BMS's delegation took to the Textile Minister.
body:
Textiles and garments are one of India's largest sources of employment, after agriculture. The sector runs from cotton farms and spinning mills to powerlooms, handlooms, processing units and garment factories. When a BMS delegation went to the Union Textile Minister on 1 September 2026, it carried the concerns of workers from several of these very different worlds. This post sets out how big the sector is, what kinds of work it contains, what the Government has done for it and what workers are asking for.

## How large is the sector

In a written reply to the Lok Sabha in December 2022, the Minister of State for Textiles said that direct employment in the textile sector was estimated at **45 million** people, and gave the industry's share of national output as around 7 per cent, citing the National Accounts Statistics. The 4th All India Handloom Census, conducted in 2019-20, counted about **35.2 lakh** persons engaged in handloom work. These are estimates, and a large part of the work is informal and counted loosely, so they are best read as a sense of scale rather than an exact figure.

## Different faces of the industry

- **Organised mills.** Composite and spinning mills, including those once owned by the National Textile Corporation, have fallen in number and have a smaller workforce than before.
- **Powerlooms.** These are decentralised, often small units, many of them in clusters, with low wages for many of the workers.
- **Handloom, silk and khadi.** These are craft traditions with strong cultural value and weak incomes for most weavers.
- **Jute.** Jute mills in eastern India employ a large workforce, many of them living in mill colonies whose condition is a standing concern.
- **Garments.** Large export-oriented clusters employ many women workers.

## The National Textile Corporation

The NTC deserves its own note because it is the Government's own mill company. It was incorporated in April 1968 to manage sick private textile undertakings that the Government had taken over, began with 16 mills and had 103 by 1972-73. The mills were nationalised in 1974 under the Sick Textile Undertakings (Nationalization) Act. By 1995 the number had reached 119. Public sources now say that NTC has closed 77 mills, has 23 working mills on its books, and has modernised 18.

BMS's account is that the picture on the ground is worse than that suggests. A BMS delegation told the Union Home Minister in June 2025 that 23 NTC mills across eight States had stopped production since the 2020 lockdown, that permanent employees were receiving half their wages and that salary had not been paid since November 2024. It asked for dues to be cleared and for production to restart in 12 selected mills. Those are BMS's statements, and the position of the Government and the company on each point should be read from their own records.

## Challenges workers and employers describe

- **Export competition and trade barriers.** Orders can move between countries quickly, and workers lose shifts or jobs when they do.
- **Raw material prices,** especially cotton, which move with weather and trade policy.
- **Technology and the cost of modernisation.** New machines raise productivity but need fewer people and different skills.
- **Wages and social security** for workers in the unorganised segment. In its meeting with the Textile Minister, BMS argued that a wage fixed on a price index alone is unjust and asked for a wage board, citing a floor-level worker in Bhilwara earning Rs 470 a day.

## Government schemes

The Government has run a number of schemes for the sector. They include the **Production Linked Incentive scheme for textiles**, aimed at high-value man-made fibre, garments and technical textiles; the **PM MITRA** scheme, which plans seven mega textile parks covering the whole value chain; the **National Handloom Development Programme**; the **SAMARTH** skilling scheme; **Silk Samagra 2**; and the Scheme for Integrated Textile Parks. Whether such schemes help workers depends on how many jobs they create and how well those jobs are paid. A park or a factory that is modern but staffed through contractors on low wages meets the investor's goal and not the worker's. That is why unions ask for conditions on wages and security to be part of the scheme's design.

## The new Labour Codes and textile work

Textile employers and workers are both affected by the four Labour Codes in force since 21 November 2025. Among their provisions, fixed-term employees are entitled to the same benefits as permanent staff and to gratuity after one year, written appointment letters are compulsory, and women may work night shifts with consent and safety measures. This last point matters in garment clusters, where women are a large share of workers. For unions, the questions are about enforcement: whether the written appointment letters are in fact given and whether the national floor wage is observed in small units.

## A long history

Textile workers also have a place in the story of India's freedom struggle. When Lokmanya Tilak was convicted of sedition in 1908, mill workers in Bombay held a six-day strike in protest, an event that drew comment even from Lenin, according to one historical summary. The industry has been a school of organised labour in India for well over a century.

## Where BMS comes in

BMS's textile and jute federations have regularly raised wages, closure of mills and the welfare of powerloom and jute workers. At the 1 September 2026 meeting, which lasted about 75 minutes according to BMS, the delegation raised pending wage dues in NTC mills, jute mill colonies and wages, support for handloom and silk weavers, mega textile parks in garment clusters and a wage board. BMS reports that the Minister responded positively, asked officials to form a special team to study jute mill labour colonies, said the Government was exploring all possible ways to settle NTC wage dues, and spoke of expanding jute cultivation by 1.5 lakh acres. BMS's note does not report a response on the wage board or on restarting the 12 mills. The demand on NTC mills was also among the eleven in the 17 August memorandum.

## What to watch

The test of that meeting is practical: whether dues are paid, whether the special team visits the colonies, and whether PM MITRA plans carry conditions on pay. Readers who work in textiles can ask their federation what has reached their own unit.
